senses: An expert on the identification and cultivation of plants.
ety: From plant + -s- + -man. Piecewise doublet of clansman.

senses: To make smaller.
To reduce in apparent size, as for example objects viewed through a lens or mirror shaped so as to increase the field of view, such as a convex or aspheric mirror or a Fresnel lens.
ety: From mini- + -fy.
examples: Schneckenburger strives to make it appear that Baur unduly minifies the Christian element in Manichæism.
There must be something in the appeal of the Gothic that minifies one group of values leaving other considerations untouched, or actually magnifying them.

senses: A mold or matrix in which anything is cast or formed to a particular shape.
ety: From Late Latin plasma (“mold”) or Ancient Greek πλάσμα (plásma, “something formed”), in some cases via German Plasma or French plasme, like English plasma.

senses: Bitten by a snake.
Experiencing a period of bad luck; unlucky.
Jumpy, as if expecting to struck by sudden misfortune.
ety: From snake + bit.
examples: Bob was feeling snakebit after losing four games.
This was followed by the BP oil spill, which made him look snakebit.

senses: To cut in advance.
ety: From pre- + cut.

senses: A streaming media delivery method which uses the Internet to deliver audio and video playback to the end user.
ety: From Web + stream.
examples: Dog lovers will be able to watch Crufts despite the BBC's decision to drop the show, thanks to a live webstream announced yesterday.

senses: Synonym of telluric current.
ety: A borrowing of French tellurique, from Latin tellus (“earth; earthy”) and Tellus (“Earth, Gaia”) and -ique (forming adjectives). Subsequently also from tellurium, originally in telluric oxide from German Telluroxyd.
examples: Other projects in progress at CRPL involve the study of audiofrequency tellurics (current induced in the earth) and earth conductivity measurements using atmospherics.

senses: A low wetland periodically flooded by salt water; a salt marsh.
ety: Borrowed from Welsh morfa.
examples: The wildlife of the morfa, the saltmarshes, reflects the diversity of their setting whilst being distinctly Welsh. There is nothing immutable about this landscape and its wildlife; its heritage is one of change.

senses: To investigate or record such characteristics.
ety: Borrowed from Russian кариотип (kariotip), equivalent to karyo- + -type.

senses: A blend of components that has been mixed in advance of use or of further processing.
A manufactured beverage consisting of alcohol and soft drink, milk or other non-alcoholic drinks; an alcopop.
ety: From pre- + mix.
examples: High velocity premix systems — high velocity premix burner systems have been popular with some European kiln builders due to the fact that they are more fuel efficient than most other systems.
As the postproduction phase nears completion, elements (units) are mixed-down to premixes (predub). Premixes are developed independently for each of the stems.
Premixes can be divided down into groups such as dialogue, effects and music, or even further, into premixes of spot effects, foley effects, atmosphere effects, etc.

senses: A traditional Mexican stone tool, equivalent in function to a mortar and pestle, used for grinding food.
ety: Borrowed from Spanish molcajete, from Classical Nahuatl mōlcaxitl.

senses: A female person who is retired from active service or an occupation, especially one who retains an honorific version of a previous title.
ety: From the Latin ēmerita, the feminine singular form of ēmeritus.
examples: With the help of ever-present chief elder Charlotte McGuire and our headquarters, an updated list of all Board members was developed. Twenty-eight persons who are now emeritae were named.

senses: strict, exact.
ety: Borrowed from Italian giusto (“right, just”). Doublet of just.

senses: To cause (a lens, or a beam of light or particles, etc.) to be out of focus.
ety: From de- + focus.

senses: A small European migratory bunting (Emberiza hortulana), once eaten whole as a delicacy.
The greater short-toed lark (Calandrella brachydactyla).
ety: From Middle French hortolan (“gardener”), from Latin hortulānus (“gardener”). Doublet of hortulan.

senses: A supporter of pietism.
ety: From piety + -ist.

senses: Someone or something that crumples.
ety: From crumple + -er.

senses: Stipa tenacissima, of North Africa.
Lygeum spartum, of the Mediterranean.
ety: From Spanish esparto, via Latin spartum from Ancient Greek σπάρτον (spárton, “rope, cable; esparto or halfah grass”), valued for its high tensile strength, used for cords and wicker, and exported by Spanish Greek colonies throughout the Mediterranian.

senses: with tight elastic folds
ety: From ruche + -ed.

senses: A secluded religious hermitage inhabited by gurus, or the population of such a hermitage.
ety: Borrowed from Sanskrit आश्रम (āśrama).
examples: In our broken culture those who have experienced the training of the yogic ashram are often woefully ignorant in the ways of the university, and vice versa.

senses: An adiabatic curve or graph
ety: 19th-century coinage (introduced by W. J. M. Rankine in the 1860s) based on Ancient Greek ἀδιάβατος (adiábatos, “impassable”), used of terrain (rivers, forests) by Xenophon, from ἀ- (a-, “not”) + διά (diá, “through”) + βατός (batós, “passable”), from βαίνω (baínō, “to go”).

senses: A small or young falcon.
ety: From falcon + -et.

senses: Commonwealth and Ireland standard spelling of fervor.
ety: By surface analysis, Latin ferv- + -our (“abstract noun suffix”).
examples: The early Americans, inheriting the Hebraist fervour of the English Puritans, had enjoyed a Great Awakening of religious joy.

senses: the mistle thrush
ety: From Middle English mistel (“mistletoe”), from Old English mistel (“mistletoe”), from Proto-West Germanic *mistil (“mistle”), from Proto-Germanic *mistilaz (“mistle”).

senses: Readily communicated.
Talkative or expansive.
ety: From Old French communicable, Latin communicabilis.

senses: A small marsupial carnivore, Myrmecobius fasciatus, endemic to western Australia, that eats almost exclusively termites.
ety: Borrowed from Nyunga nhumbad.

senses: One who tends bees, usually as an occupation; beekeeper.
ety: From Middle English beman, bemon, perhaps a partial calque of Old English bēoċeorl (“beekeeper”), equivalent to bee + -man. Old English bēoċeorl may be an alteration of bēocere (“beekeeper”).
examples: I am a beeman of long standing, having practically kept bees all my life.

senses: To cause (a dog, horse, or other four-legged mammal) to dislocate or sprain its stifle joint.
ety: The noun is derived from Middle English stifle (“joint between the femur and tibia of a quadruped”) [and other forms]; further etymology uncertain, probably derived from Anglo-Norman estive (“leg”), and Old French estive (“leg”) (compare Old French estival (“boot, shoe”)). The verb is derived from the noun.

senses: A ceremony at some European universities to confer a Doctor of Divinity degree.
ety: From Latin aulicus (“of a prince's court”), from aula (“royal court”), from Ancient Greek αὐλή (aulḗ, “courtyard”).

senses: Belonging to, or relating to, elves.
ety: From elf + -en. Compare elfin, elven.
examples: ALFHILD. Were I an elfen maid, then truly, say I, it would fare with you ill! / OLAF. Forsooth, then are you the elfen maid!

senses: A non-contact unisex team sport originating from the Netherlands, similar to netball, where players attempt to throw a ball into a basket atop a pole.
The ball used in the sport of korfball.
ety: Borrowing from Dutch korfbal. Equivalent to corf + ball.

senses: A kind of manga written for an older male audience, generally 18-30 years old (and older).
ety: Borrowed from Japanese 青年 (seinen).

senses: Describing a cooling or moisturizing lotion applied to the skin after exposure to the sun, especially to soothe sunburn.
ety: From after- + sun.
examples: Apply aftersun lotion to avoid peeling and flaking caused by sun damage.

senses: A household or religious community under one head, regarded as a unit.
ety: Learned borrowing from Latin familia (“family”). Doublet of family.

senses: Grandmother.
ety: From grand- + mom.

senses: A small civilian settlement outside a Roman fort.
ety: Borrowed from Latin vīcus (“village”). Doublet of wick.

senses: The act of captivating or the state of being captivated.
ety: From captivate + -ion.
examples: But the test of an oration is not only its immediate effect; there are tricks of elocution, a jugglery of manner, and even a personal captivation that so win the senses as to bewilder the judgment.

senses: Born on or in the sea.
ety: From sea + born.

senses: A white meat stew in which neither the meat nor the sauce is browned.
ety: Borrowed from French blanquette, from Provençal blanqueto, a diminutive of blanc (“white”), derived, through early Medieval Latin blancus, from Frankish *blank (“gleaming, white, blinding”), from Proto-Germanic *blankaz (“white, bright, blinding”), from Proto-Indo-European *bhleg- (“to shine”). Compare blanket.

senses: The team which supports the matador.
ety: From Spanish cuadrilla (“team”). Doublet of quadrille.
